learn.hook: Look up at a kite or down from a balcony — the angle your eyes turn through is the key to measuring things you can't reach!
points: The line of sight is the straight line from your eye to the object you are looking at.
Angle of elevation: the angle between the horizontal and the line of sight when you look UP at an object.
Angle of depression: the angle between the horizontal and the line of sight when you look DOWN at an object.
The angle of elevation of A from B equals the angle of depression of B from A — they are alternate angles between parallel horizontal lines.
As you walk towards a tower, the angle of elevation of its top increases. If the height equals the distance, the angle is 45°.

example.q: A kite is flying on a 100 m string that makes an angle of 30° with the ground. How high is the kite? (Assume the string is straight.)
steps: The string is the hypotenuse; the height is opposite the 30° angle

learn.reallife: During Makar Sankranti, kite flyers can estimate how high their kite is from the string length and the angle it makes with the ground.

games.title: Line-of-sight check
items: The angle of elevation is measured from the horizontal.
It is the angle between the horizontal line and the line of sight.
The angle of depression of a point P from the top of a tower equals the angle of elevation of the top from P.
They are alternate angles between parallel horizontal lines.
As you walk towards a tower, the angle of elevation of its top decreases.
It increases — the top looks steeper as you get closer.
If a tower's height equals your distance from its foot, the angle of elevation is 45°.
tan θ = height/distance = 1, so θ = 45°.
The angle of depression is measured from the vertical line.
It is measured down from the horizontal line.
A longer shadow of the same pole means the sun is lower in the sky.
A smaller angle of elevation of the sun gives a longer shadow.

quiz.q: A tower's height equals the distance of a point from its foot. What is the angle of elevation of the top from that point?
quiz.explain: tan θ = height/distance = 1, so θ = 45°.
quiz.mistake: Thinks equal sides give 60° as in an equilateral triangle

quiz.q: A kite flies on a 60 m string at an angle of elevation of 30°. How high is it?
quiz.explain: sin 30° = height/60, so height = 60 × 1/2 = 30 m.
quiz.mistake: Uses cos 30° and gets 30√3 m

quiz.q: A 10 m pole casts a shadow 10√3 m long. What is the sun's angle of elevation?
quiz.mistake: Computes shadow/height and gets 60°

quiz.q: From the top of a 20 m building, the angle of depression of a scooter on the road is 45°. How far is the scooter from the building?
quiz.explain: The angle of elevation of the top from the scooter is also 45°. tan 45° = 20/d = 1, so d = 20 m.
quiz.mistake: Uses sin or cos instead of tan, or puts the distance on top of the fraction

quiz.q: Why is the angle of depression of B from A equal to the angle of elevation of A from B?
options: They are alternate angles between parallel horizontal lines
quiz.explain: The horizontal lines through A and B are parallel, and the line AB is a transversal, so the two angles are alternate angles.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up alternate and vertically opposite angles

quiz.q: The sun's angle of elevation rises from 30° to 60°. What happens to the shadow of a flagpole?
quiz.explain: shadow = height/tan θ. tan 60° is bigger than tan 30°, so the shadow gets shorter.
quiz.mistake: Thinks a higher sun makes a longer shadow

quiz.q: A 6 m ladder leans against a wall and reaches a height of 3√3 m. What angle does it make with the ground?
quiz.mistake: Uses cos instead of sin and gets 30°

quiz.q: Kabir's eyes are 1.6 m above the ground. He stands 18.4 m from a flagpole and sees its top at an angle of elevation of 45°. How tall is the flagpole?
quiz.explain: Above eye level the height is 18.4 × tan 45° = 18.4 m. Add his eye height: 18.4 + 1.6 = 20 m.
quiz.mistake: Forgets to add the height of Kabir's eyes

teach.ask: Gappu is on a tree looking down at a worm: 'Is this an angle of elevation or depression? How is it measured?'
teach.praise: Tweet! Measure from the horizontal — up is elevation, down is depression. Worm spotted!
teach.nudge: From which line do I measure the angle, and does it matter whether I look up or down?

learn.hook: Find the height of a temple gopuram or a mobile tower without climbing a single step!
points: Draw a neat figure: the object is vertical, the ground is horizontal, so you get a right triangle.
Use tan θ = height/distance when you know the distance along the ground.
Use sin θ = height/hypotenuse when you know a slanting length, like a ladder or a kite string.
If the observer's eye is above the ground, add the eye height to the height found from the triangle.
For two angles seen from two places, write one equation for each triangle and solve them together.

example.q: From a point 30 m from the foot of a temple gopuram, the angle of elevation of its top is 60°. Find its height.

learn.reallife: Engineers check the height of electric poles and water tanks using an instrument called a clinometer, which measures angles of elevation.

items.q: Height above eye level 28.5 m, eye height 1.5 m. Total height?
A 2√3 m ladder makes 60° with the ground. Height reached (in m)?

games.title: Steps to find a tree's height
games.prompt: The top of a tree is seen at 60° elevation from a point 15 m away
items: Draw right triangle ABC: tree AB, point C on the ground, ∠C = 60°
Pick the ratio linking height and ground distance: tan 60° = AB/BC
Substitute: √3 = AB/15

quiz.q: From a point 40 m from the foot of a water tower, the angle of elevation of its top is 30°. How tall is the tower?
quiz.mistake: Uses tan 60° (√3) instead of tan 30°

quiz.q: A storm bends a tree so that its top touches the ground 6 m from the foot, making an angle of 30° with the ground. How tall was the tree?
quiz.explain: Standing part = 6 tan 30° = 2√3 m. Broken part = 6/cos 30° = 4√3 m. Total = 6√3 m (about 10.39 m).
quiz.mistake: Finds only the standing part (2√3 m) and forgets the broken part

quiz.q: A kite flies on an 80 m string at an angle of elevation of 60°. How high is the kite?
quiz.mistake: Uses cos 60° and gets 40 m

quiz.q: A pole casts a 5 m shadow when the sun's elevation is 60°. Using √3 = 1.73, how tall is the pole?
quiz.mistake: Divides by √3 instead of multiplying

quiz.q: From a point 20 m from a building, the top of the building is at 45° elevation and the top of a flagpole on it is at 60°. How long is the flagpole?
quiz.explain: Building height = 20 tan 45° = 20 m. Height to flagpole top = 20 tan 60° = 20√3 m. Flagpole = 20√3 − 20 = 20(√3 − 1) m.
quiz.mistake: Gives the total height instead of subtracting the building

quiz.q: You know a ladder's length and the angle it makes with the ground. Which ratio gives the height it reaches?
quiz.explain: Height is opposite the angle and the ladder is the hypotenuse, so use sin θ = height/ladder.
quiz.mistake: Uses tan, which needs the ground distance instead

quiz.q: A gopuram is seen at an angle of elevation of 30° from 50 m away. Using √3 = 1.732, about how tall is it?
quiz.mistake: Multiplies by √3 instead of dividing

quiz.q: From the top of a 10 m building, the angle of elevation of a tower's top is 30°. From the building's foot it is 60°. How tall is the tower?
quiz.explain: Let the tower be H and the gap d. From the foot: H = d√3. From the top: H − 10 = d/√3 = H/3. So 2H/3 = 10 and H = 15 m.
quiz.mistake: Forgets to subtract the building height in the upper triangle

teach.ask: Gappu wants to know how tall the school's water tank is: 'How can I find it from the ground?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Measure the angle and the distance, then height = distance × tan. No ladder needed!
teach.nudge: What two things do I measure from the ground, and which ratio joins them?

learn.hook: A lighthouse keeper can tell how far a boat is just by looking down at it — let's learn how!
points: For angle of depression θ from height h, the horizontal distance is d = h/tan θ.
At 45° the distance equals the height; at 30° it is h√3 (farther); at 60° it is h/√3 (closer).
A bigger angle of depression means the object is closer to the foot of the tower.
For an object that moves, find the distance at each angle and subtract.
If you walk a known distance towards a tower, set up two triangles that share the same height.

example.q: From the top of a 60 m lighthouse, the angle of depression of a boat is 30°. How far is the boat from the lighthouse?
steps: The angle of elevation of the top from the boat is also 30°

learn.reallife: Coast guards and air traffic controllers estimate how far boats and planes are using angles and heights.

games.title: Match the distance
pairs: Angle of depression of a boat from the top
Equals the angle of elevation of the top from the boat

items.text: From a 30 m tower at a depression of 30°, the distance = 30 × ___
As the angle of depression of a car increases, the car is coming ___ the tower
From tan θ = height/distance, distance = height ÷ ___

quiz.q: From the top of a 50 m cliff, the angle of depression of a boat is 45°. How far is the boat from the foot of the cliff?
quiz.mistake: Uses sin 45° or cos 45° instead of tan

quiz.q: From the top of a 60 m tower, the angle of depression of a car changes from 30° to 60° as it drives towards the tower. How far did the car travel?
quiz.mistake: Gives only one of the two distances

quiz.q: From a balcony 9 m high, the angle of depression of a car is 30°. Using √3 = 1.73, how far is the car from the building?
quiz.mistake: Divides by √3 and gets 5.2 m

quiz.q: The angle of elevation of a tower's top is 30° from a point. After walking 20 m towards the tower it becomes 60°. How tall is the tower?
quiz.explain: Let the new distance be d. h = d√3 and h = (d + 20)/√3. So 3d = d + 20, d = 10 m and h = 10√3 m (≈ 17.32 m).
quiz.mistake: Uses 20 m as the distance in the 60° triangle

quiz.q: A tower's top is at 30° elevation from a point. After walking 30 m towards it, the elevation becomes 60°. How far is the second point from the tower?
quiz.explain: With d the new distance: d√3 = (d + 30)/√3, so 3d = d + 30 and d = 15 m.
quiz.mistake: Assumes the walk covered the whole distance to the tower

quiz.q: From the top of a 100 m tower, the angle of depression of a car is 60°. Using √3 = 1.732, how far is the car from the tower?
quiz.mistake: Multiplies by √3 and gets 173.2 m

quiz.q: From the top of a tower, the angle of depression of a stone on the ground is 30°. Which is longer?
options: The stone's distance from the foot of the tower
quiz.explain: d = h/tan 30° = h√3, and √3 > 1, so the horizontal distance is longer than the height.
quiz.mistake: Thinks a small angle means the stone is close

quiz.q: Two ships are on the same side of a 100 m lighthouse, in line with its foot. The angles of depression are 45° and 60°. Using √3 = 1.732, how far apart are the ships?
quiz.explain: The 45° ship is 100 m away and the 60° ship is 100/√3 ≈ 57.74 m away. The gap is 100 − 57.74 = 42.26 m.
quiz.mistake: Adds the distances as if the ships were on opposite sides

teach.ask: Gappu sits on top of a lighthouse looking at a boat: 'How can I know how far the boat is?'
teach.praise: Tweet tweet! Distance = height ÷ tan of the angle. The boat is no mystery now!
teach.nudge: Which two things do I know from the lighthouse, and how do they give the distance?

topics.title: Poles across a road, balloons, birds — and chapter recap

learn.hook: A bird flies off a treetop, a balloon drifts in the wind, two poles face each other across a road — one ratio, tan, solves them all!
points: Two poles across a road: let the unknown distance from one pole be x; the other is (width − x). Write tan for each triangle with the same height h and solve.
Moving objects at a fixed height (a bird flying level, a drifting balloon): find the horizontal distance at each angle and subtract. Speed = distance ÷ time.
Ropes and ladders are slant lengths, so use sin (height = rope × sin θ) or cos (ground distance = rope × cos θ).
In Class 10 problems, angles are only 30°, 45° and 60°, and at most two right triangles are used. Use √3 ≈ 1.732 when asked for a decimal.
Recap: line of sight; angle of elevation (looking up) and depression (looking down) are equal for the same pair of points; choose the ratio that links the known and unknown sides.

example.q: Two poles of equal height stand on opposite sides of a road 100 m wide. From a point on the road between them, the angles of elevation of their tops are 60° and 30°. Find the height of the poles.
steps: Let the point be x m from the first pole (60°), so (100 − x) m from the other (30°)
example.answer: Each pole is 25√3 m ≈ 43.3 m high

learn.reallife: Traffic engineers place street lights on both sides of a road at heights that light up the middle — the same two-triangle problem!

games.title: Two poles across a road
items: Draw both poles and the point between them
Call the distance to one pole x and to the other (width − x)
Write tan of each angle = h ÷ its distance
Equate the two expressions for h and solve for x
Substitute x back to find h

quiz.q: Two poles of equal height stand on opposite sides of a 100 m road. From a point between them the angles of elevation of their tops are 60° and 30°. How high are the poles?
quiz.explain: h = √3x and h = (100 − x)/√3 give 3x = 100 − x, so x = 25 and h = 25√3 m.
quiz.mistake: Assumes the point is in the middle of the road

quiz.q: In the same problem, how far is the point from the pole whose top is seen at 60°?
quiz.explain: From 3x = 100 − x, x = 25 m. The point is closer to the pole seen at the larger angle.
quiz.mistake: Gives the distance to the other pole

quiz.q: Riya's eyes are 1.5 m above the ground. A balloon flying at 51.5 m is first seen at 45° elevation and, after drifting level, at 30°. Using √3 = 1.732, how far did it drift?
quiz.explain: Height above her eyes = 50 m. Distances: 50/tan 45° = 50 m and 50/tan 30° = 50√3 ≈ 86.6 m. Drift ≈ 86.6 − 50 = 36.6 m.
quiz.mistake: Forgets to subtract the eye height, or gives one distance instead of the difference

quiz.q: A bird sits on top of a 20 m tree; from a point on the ground its angle of elevation is 45°. It flies away level, and 2 seconds later the angle is 30°. Using √3 = 1.732, what is the bird's speed in m/s?
quiz.explain: Distances: 20 m (at 45°) and 20√3 ≈ 34.64 m (at 30°). It flew 14.64 m in 2 s, so the speed is 7.32 m/s.
quiz.mistake: Gives the distance flown instead of dividing by the time

quiz.q: A 16 m rope is stretched tight from the top of a vertical pole to the ground, making 30° with the ground. How tall is the pole?
quiz.explain: The rope is the hypotenuse, so height = 16 × sin 30° = 16 × 1/2 = 8 m.
quiz.mistake: Uses cos or tan instead of sin

quiz.q: In Class 10 heights-and-distances problems, which angles of elevation or depression are used?
quiz.explain: The syllabus restricts problems to 30°, 45° and 60°, with at most two right triangles.
quiz.mistake: Thinks any angle may appear

quiz.q: From the top of a 12 m building, the angle of elevation of the top of a taller building across the road is 30°, and the angle of depression of its foot is 45°. Using √3 = 1.732, how tall is the taller building?
quiz.explain: 45° depression → road width = 12 m. Extra height above 12 m = 12 tan 30° = 12/√3 ≈ 6.93 m. Total ≈ 18.93 m.
quiz.mistake: Forgets to add the height of the first building

quiz.q: A 6 m pole and a 10 m pole stand 4 m apart on level ground. What is the angle of elevation of the top of the taller pole from the top of the shorter one?
quiz.explain: The height difference is 10 − 6 = 4 m and the gap is 4 m, so tan θ = 4/4 = 1 and θ = 45°.
quiz.mistake: Uses the full height 10 m instead of the difference

teach.ask: Gappu sees two equal poles across a road and wants their height. He knows the road width and both angles. Explain how to set it up.
teach.praise: Chirp! Split the road into x and (width − x), write tan for each side with the same h, and solve!
teach.nudge: What is the same in both triangles?
